Puzzle 16 · 17 of 23

The main thread's queue

Messages arrive on Binder threads, but screen code must run on the main thread. So everything for the screen waits in one line, and the main thread takes it one by one.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 6: You don't call. You're called.

    system_server decides → Binder carries the message → your main thread receives it → your code runs. You write onCreate(); you never call it.

  • Puzzle 12: Sharing memory without sharing mistakes

    Memory comes in pages. After a fork, parent and child share every page; a page is copied only when one of them writes to it: copy-on-write.

  • Puzzle 15: Inside a Binder call

    proxy → Parcel → Binder stamps your UID → a Binder thread → the real method, and back. Meanwhile the thread that called waits.

The problem

In puzzle 15, a Binder thread picked up the town hall's message. But in puzzle 2, only the main thread could touch the screen. Why only one thread? Puzzle 3: the screen has one owner, because two threads changing the same text at once could break it. So how does the message get from the Binder thread to the main thread?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

The main thread has an in-tray: its message queue. (A message from Binder becomes a message in this queue: the Binder thread puts it there.) Every piece of screen work waits there as a message: draw the screen, handle a touch, run a lifecycle callback. Touches arrive in this queue too, by their own road (puzzle 17).

The Looper is the main thread's endless loop, the one in the picture above: take the next message, run it to the end, repeat. A Handler is an object tied to one thread's queue that drops messages into it. The ones on this page are tied to the main thread's queue: the Binder thread uses one, then goes back to waiting (it doesn't wait for the main thread), and handler.post { … }post() wraps your code in a Message and puts it in this Handler's queue. 438 public final boolean post(@NonNull Runnable r) { 439 return sendMessageDelayed(getPostMessage(r), 0); 440 } … 782 private boolean enqueueMessage(@NonNull MessageQueue queue, @NonNull Message msg, 783 long uptimeMillis) { 784 msg.target = this; … 789 }Handler.java, line 438 · AOSP frameworks/base ↗ is how you drop your own code in. The analogy

The clerk at the front desk has an in-tray. Couriers drop letters in through the slot; the clerk takes one at a time and finishes it before the next.

Check yourself

Two Binder threads receive a message for your screen at the same moment. Can your buttons and text be changed by both at once?

Not quite. Neither Binder thread touches the screen: they post to the queue, and only the main thread runs it.

Right. The queue turns many senders into one worker, in order.

What does handler.post { … }post() wraps your code in a Message and puts it in this Handler's queue. 438 public final boolean post(@NonNull Runnable r) { 439 return sendMessageDelayed(getPostMessage(r), 0); 440 } … 782 private boolean enqueueMessage(@NonNull MessageQueue queue, @NonNull Message msg, 783 long uptimeMillis) { 784 msg.target = this; … 789 }Handler.java, line 438 · AOSP frameworks/base ↗ do?

Right. A Handler is the slot into the queue.

Not quite. A Handler starts nothing: it drops a message into one queue.

What's the difference between a Binder thread and the main thread?

Not quite. The courier receives; the clerk does the work. The Binder thread hands over through the queue.

Right. Couriers receive; one clerk works.

What you now know

Binder thread → Handler → the main thread's message queue → the Looper runs it. One message at a time, in order, so buttons and text never need a lock.
